paper.title: Low-Resource Transliteration for Roman-Urdu and Urdu Using Transformer-Based Models
paper.abstract: As the Information Retrieval (IR) field increasingly recognizes the importance of inclusivity, addressing the needs of low-resource languages remains a significant challenge. Transliteration between Urdu and its Romanized form, Roman Urdu, remains underexplored despite the widespread use of both scripts in South Asia. Prior work using RNNs on the Roman-Urdu-Parl dataset showed promising results but suffered from poor domain adaptability and limited evaluation. We propose a transformer-based approach using the m2m100 multilingual translation model, enhanced with masked language modeling (MLM) pretraining and fine-tuning on both Roman-Urdu-Parl and the domain-diverse Dakshina dataset. To address previous evaluation flaws, we introduce rigorous dataset splits and assess performance using BLEU, character-level BLEU, and CHRF. Our model achieves strong transliteration performance, with Char-BLEU scores of 96.37 for Urdu->Roman-Urdu and 97.44 for Roman-Urdu->Urdu. These results outperform both RNN baselines and GPT-4o Mini and demonstrate the effectiveness of multilingual transfer learning for low-resource transliteration tasks.

summary.one_line: The paper presents a transformer-based model for transliterating between Urdu and Roman Urdu, achieving high character-level BLEU scores.
summary.problem: Low-resource transliteration between Urdu and its Romanized form is underexplored and existing RNN approaches lack domain adaptability and proper evaluation. The paper aims to improve transliteration quality and evaluation rigor for these scripts.
summary.method: The authors fine-tune the m2m100 multilingual translation model with masked language modeling pretraining, using the Roman-Urdu-Parl and Dakshina datasets. They introduce strict dataset splits and evaluate with BLEU, character-level BLEU, and CHRF metrics.
summary.result: The model attains Char-BLEU scores of 96.37 for Urdu→Roman Urdu and 97.44 for Roman Urdu→Urdu, surpassing RNN baselines and GPT-4o Mini.
summary.why_it_matters: Improved transliteration supports inclusive information retrieval for low-resource languages, enabling better access to digital content for Urdu speakers using both scripts.

medium:
## Transliteration Made Easy: A Transformer Wins Over RNNs for Urdu Scripts 
*How a simple fine-tune turned a multilingual model into a specialist for Roman-Urdu.* 

I was scrolling through the latest arXiv submissions on a rainy Tuesday, looking for anything that could help my friend who writes code comments in Roman Urdu but needs to generate Urdu documentation automatically. The title caught my eye because I have seen countless RNN-based transliteration tools stumble over spelling variations and informal slang. I clicked, skimmed the abstract, and then dug into the methodology. The authors’ approach felt refreshingly pragmatic: they took a large multilingual translation model, gave it a brief masked-language-modeling warm-up on two Urdu datasets, and then evaluated it with strict train-test splits. The whole process reminded me of how a generalist can become a specialist with just the right data.

**Hook line** 
A transformer that was built for dozens of languages can now transliterate Urdu and Roman Urdu with near-perfect character accuracy.

**What the paper is about** 
The authors address the low-resource problem of converting between Urdu script and its Romanized form. They fine-tune the m2m100 multilingual model, first pretraining it with masked language modeling on the Roman-Urdu-Parl and Dakshina corpora. They also introduce strict dataset splits and evaluate the system with BLEU, character-level BLEU and CHRF metrics.

**What they found** 
The fine-tuned model reaches a character-level BLEU of 96.37 for Urdu → Roman Urdu and 97.44 for the reverse direction, beating the RNN baselines and even GPT-4o Mini. 

**Why I read it and what I took away** 
I read this paper because I needed a reliable way to bridge the two scripts that my team encounters daily. The most striking lesson for me is that a well-chosen multilingual backbone, when paired with a small amount of domain-specific pretraining, can outperform purpose-built RNNs and even large language models on a narrow task. It suggests that I can repurpose other multilingual models for niche transliteration problems without building everything from scratch. I also appreciated the authors’ emphasis on strict train-test splits; it reminded me to be more rigorous when I benchmark my own tools.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.21530v2 

**One real question** 
How does the model handle code-mixed sentences where Urdu and Roman Urdu appear side by side, a common pattern in social media posts?
